WATCHING LIKE A HAWK

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
There is a new Hawks soaring high above and watching closely. Will the tide in the investigations of especially corruption finally start to turn? Adv Godfrey Lebeay is bad news for organised crime.

Unique Selling Point:
There is a new Hawks soaring high above and watching closely. Will the tide in the investigations of especially corruption finally start to turn? Adv Godfrey Lebeay is bad news for organised crime - or at least, this is what South Africans are hoping for.
Who is this man who is an admitted advocate, has a doctorate in organised crime and seems completely affable, open, soft-spoken and warm? And will he finally be the one who will stamp his authority and clean up the rotten mess in one of the criminal justice system's most important legs?

Further information:
For more than a year the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, better known as the Hawks has been without a permanent head. The unit has been dogged with perception of political interference especially in high-profile appointments for years.
The Hawks has had four head since its inception after the Scorpions disbandment in 2009 and adv. Godfrey Lebeya's appointment is regarded as a new dawn within the unit.
His appointment comes at a critical time in turning the tide of the endemic corruption of the Zuma years. Lebeya, once sidelined by former SAPS National Commissioner Riah Phiyega, is highly respected. But he will have his work cut out for him rebuilding a directorate that has been put under much suspicion by his predecessor, Berning Ntlemeza.
He replaces Lt-Gen Yolisa Matakata, who was appointed acting Hawks head by former police minister Fikile Mbalula in April 2017 after the appointment of Maj-Gen Berning Ntlemeza to the position was ruled to have irregular and unlawful. Matakata had stood in after the controversy around former Hawks head Bernard Ntlemeza.
In March 2015, the High Court in Pretoria found that Ntlemeza lied under oath, mislead the court and lacked integrity and honour. The High Court struck his case from the roll, saying his appointment was irrational and unlawful. He was forced to vacate his office after the High Court, in Pretoria, turned down an application by Ntlemeza to turn to the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein in a bid to cling to his position as the head of the Directorate of Priority Crimes Investigation.
Following the court ruling, Mbalula called for unity within the police. He said he hoped finality in the Ntlemeza matter brought an end to factionalism within the police. He warned that Ntlemeza is now considered to be on the outside of the organisation and was demanding the officers be professional and reject the idea of being part of what he terms "rogue cabals". Former Minister Mbalula publicly stated he planned to drive out corrupt elements out of the controversial crime intelligence unit.
But Ntlemeza's legal woes were far from over. The High Court ruling formed the basis of an application to have his appointment as head of the Hawks set aside on the ground that he was fit to hold the position. Ntlemeza state in a sworn affidavit that former KZN Hawks boss, Johan Booysen was party to the process to appoint his successor and that he was also interviewed as a candidate, but as Booysen pointed out in a supplementary affidavit, this claim was not true. Ntlemeza filed a follow-up statement saying that he had signed an incorrect draft affidavit which included the error, without reading it.
Ntlemeza was also accused of attempting to mislead the Supreme Court of Appeal in a statement he made to the SCA to appeal the KwaZulu-Natal High Court's rejection of his appeal in the matter involving Booysen. Ntlemeza made inaccurate comments in an affidavit to the SCA and described the inaccurate comments as a bona fide error.
In June 2016, the SCA ruled that Ntlemeza's appointment should be set aside. In his letter to the constitutional court, Ntlemeza said that he was only made aware of the June ruling of the SCA in September.
At the time, Booysen said this explanation was incredulous and couldn't be believed, considering that Ntlemeza was a Lieutenant-General who was the head of the Hawks and should know the gravity of deposing to an affidavit.
He said for Ntlemeza to claim that he did not read the affidavit made a mockery of the legislation because this would become a convenient excuse for anyone lying under oath in written statements.
Further to this, Ntlemeza wrote to the constitutional court for leave to appeal his removal from the Hawks and he also wanted former Police Minister Fikile Mbalula to reinstate him while awaiting the outcome of the Constitutional Court application.
In September 2017, Ntlemeza lost his final court bid to overturn his dismissal. The SCA dismissed his application for leave to appeal the decision setting aside his appointment. At the time, the Police Ministiry said Ntlemeza's employment contract was set aside, as if it never existed. Former Police Minister Mbalula said that meant Ntlemeza was considered retired at a lower rank.
Praise for Lt Gen Lebeya's appointment streamed in. He comes with an impressive record. Not only has Lt Gen Lebeya been a career policeman for 37 years, he also has four law degrees, was ad advocate with the Johannesburg bar and did his highly-regarded doctorate in organized crime. His thesis flowed to a book about organized crime, on not only academic, but also practical level on how organized crime should be tackled in South Africa.
Lebeya, former head of detective services, was also the deputy commissioner of the Crime Intelligence unit from February 2011 to May 2016 when he was irregularly dismissed by former Police Commission Riah Phiyega in 2014.
He and another high-ranking officer were caught up in a legal wrangle over the dismissals and they'd won a large settlement after being illegally fired by former top cop Riah Phiyega. But his service was terminated nonetheless. Lebeya was also one of the senior officers alleged to have been involved in a conspiracy against former crime intelligence boss Richard Mdluli - a claim that was found by the high court to have no substance. As the deputy commissioner of Crime Intelligence he'd insisted that the investigation into Mdluli continue, but he bumped heads with especially Phiyega.
It was because of Mdluli, who was close to Jacob Zuma, that Lebeya was sidelined by Phiyega in 2014 while he oversaw an internal investigation into maladministration in the Crime Intelligence division. Lebeya was appointed as the deputy commissioner during Bheki Cele's time as Police Commissioner in 2011. Phiyega first demoted Lebeya and then fired him. Lebeya later won a settlement when Phiyega's action was deemed illegal by the labour court.
Lebeya, along with Bheki Cele, Gauteng provincial police commissioner Mzwandile Petros, and then Hawks Head Anwa Dramat, were all named by Mdluli in a 2011 letter to Jacob Zuma accusing the officers of colluding to unseat him as head of Crime Intelligence.
Mdluli faced fraud and corruption charges related to the abuse of a massive crime intelligence division slush fund for private benefit, including buying luxury cars. Phiyega refused to declassify crucial evidence in the Mdluli matter. The NGO Freedom Under Law said that the failure by Phiyega to declassify the documents had allowed Mdluli to "get away scot-free both at SAPS and in a court of law".
Former Gauteng Hawks head Shadrack Sibiya, tasked by Lebeya to investigate the murder of Oupa Ramogibe, who allegedly had an affair with Mdluli's former partner, said the investigation had later cost him his job. Mdluli and his co-accused, former police officer Mthembeni Mthunzi, faced charges of intimidation, kidnapping, assault with the intent to commit grievous bodily harm and defeating the ends of justice. These as well as the other charges relating to the Crime Intelligence slush fund were later withdrawn by acting NPA head Nomgcobo Jiba - who was struck off the advocates roll in 2016. The charges against Mdluli were later reinstated in 2015 following a ruling by the SCA.
In 2015, Lebeya was one of five candidates who made it to the initial shortlist of possible new heads of the Hawks. The short-listing panel was chaired by then Police Minister Nathi Nhleko. The desperately under-qualified Berning Ntlemeza, who was not on the shortlist, was catapulted into the job by Nhleko, who then took more than a year to inform Parliament that he had given Ntlemeza the job. Ntlemeza immediately set about eviscerating the directorate of qualified senior staff. He was also responsible for suspending Sibiya in 2015, which was later declared unconstitutional and invalid. Ntlemeza was finally given the boot by former Police Minister Mbalula in 2017, bringing to an end to a shameful and disastrous two years for the DPCI, during which it also hounded then finance Minister Pravin Gordhan on trumped-up charges relating to the SARS "rogue-unit".
Now, the rot of corruption is deep and has spread to all levels of society, especially in SOEs like Eskom, Prasa, SARS, to municipalities - all brought to the brink of collapse by corrupt officials and political cronies.
Violent crime has spiked, cash-in-transit heists are at a record high.
Experts say everyone expect that Lebeya's appointment will bring miracles at a fast speed, but he first needs to sweep clean - look into those appointments that were made due to political influence and set the record straight to be able to build a strong team under him. And then he needs to refocus to rebuild the unit into what it is supposed to do and do well - to investigate priority crime at the highest of levels - no easy task. But he was a deputy commissioner for Crime Intelligence and he was the head of detective services. He knows what it would require.
Lt Gen Lebeya, who is highly regarded by his peers, was also one of the candidates to replace Thuli Madonsela as public protector. His appointment as Hawks boss was announced along with a string of other posts, including a permanent head for Crime Intelligence and a permanent National Police Commissioner. Lt Gen Lebeya's appointment follows years of accusations that the elite investigating unit had been politicised.

Press Release:


The Hawks: A New Dawn?

For years organised crime and corruption has been rampant in South Africa and the Hawks, which targets criminal syndicates and other economic crimes, has been accused of been ineffective. Now with a doctorate in law and three decades of service in the police, General Godfrey Lebeya has been appointed to lead this elite crime fighting unit. Can the man who was once in the running for Public Protector, clean up the rot in one of the most important offices in the criminal justice system?

Producer: Este de Klerk

Presenter: Derek Watts

Researcher: Siniketiwe Hlanze

Script:


PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK
PRESENTER: DEREK WATTS
EDITOR: ROBIN LEUCI
BROADCAST DATE: 17 JUNE 2018

[START WITH SEQUENCE OF VIOLENT CRIMES]

South Africans live in fear of the serious violent crimes which continue to threaten society: From armed robberies, murders, car-hijackings, the recent spike in cash-in-transit heists, and the decimation of state-owned enterprises through corrupt officials and state capture

[show another short sequence of violent crimes]

BHEKI CELE: 2010/2011 people have forgotten about cash-heists, you go and see your stats It was a really rare happening unlike today. when it comes to murders, we are back to 19 000 in the year from 16 000, we are back to daily car-hijacking. Why it has happened, how it has happened, don't ask me, I wasn't there.

VO: As part of police minister Bheki Cele's plan to clean up the country's crime fighting units, General Godfrey Lebeya has been appointed as the new head of the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, the Hawks - a man the minister selected to be deputy commissioner in charge of crime intelligence and detective services in 2011 when he was police commissioner.

BHEKI CELE: The biggest advantage with him, the man has been almost 32 years on the game, he was once a deputy head, he is not new there, highly decorated when it comes to education, knows the law very well.

VO: It's clear that the new Hawks boss has been burning the midnight oil since he took office on the 1st of June. We met this warm and affable career policeman at his office at seven in the evening - the only gap he could find for the interview and the first he's granted to the media since his appointment.

[DEREK & LEBEYA MEETING AND SHAKING HANDS]

DEREK: General, did you have much sleep over the last two weeks?

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: I must say that I have not. I have been thinking about the task ahead of me, so that kept me awake most of the time. I feel honoured that I've been called again to come and join others who are fighting corruption.

BHEKI CELE: He never goes to sleep before he finishes, cleans his desk. He is a man that will never, and whenever when you make the call he will ask is: Do you need me? When you say: Yes! It doesn't matter what time of the day, he will be there.

DEREK LINK: WHILE THE APPOINTMENT OF GENERAL LEBEYA HAS BEEN WIDELY ENDORSED AND HIS PEDIGREE IS IMPRESSIVE...THE QUESTION REMAINS...HOW CAN HE GO ABOUT REMOVING THE PARASITES FROM THE HAWKS NEST

VO: With refreshing candor, General Lebeya is quick to admit the Hawks he took over is not the elite crime fighting unit it's supposed to be.

DEREK: Some say that the country's ability to fight crime has been totally decimated.
GENERAL GODFREY LEBEYA: The performance of the Hawks as of now, the latest, is not the same as the performance of the Hawks in 2011. What went wrong? We are seeking answers as of now and I think that when I say I'm doing assessment, I'm also looking at answers and I know that pretty soon, we will to a certain extent know where did we go wrong.
DEREK: What are your immediate priorities?
GENERAL GODFREY LEBEYA: The immediate priorities are those that is a burning issue to the people of South Africa. I hear and see what the rest of South Africans are seeing.
DEREK LINK: WITH THE HAWKS IMPLICATED IN A NUMBER OF SERIOUS CRIMES, ALONG WITH DRAGGING THEIR FEET IN STATE CAPTURE INVESTIGATIONS, THEIR PUBLIC IMAGE IS AT AN ALL TIME LOW AS GENERAL LEBEYA TAKES THE HOT SEAT
Dr Johan Burger, senior researcher of the Institute of Security Studies has known general Lebeya for the past 20 years. He says South Africa can be assured that this new Hawks Head will be watching closely and will act decisively against the country's toughest criminals.

DR BURGER: The Hawks generally are perceived as inefficient, as corrupt, as also complicit in a number of crimes themselves. Now the new incumbents have to fix the leadership within their various components of the police service and at the same time make them more effective.

VO: General Lebeya is determined to restore the image of the Hawks as an elite and successful crime fighting unit.

DEREK: what do you feel that you can bring to this job?

GENERAL LEBEYA: some of the things that I need to be bringing into this job is integrity. I need those who are working with me to understand that corruption is something that can't visit the Hawks. the community should trust us and that is how we shall obviously be building this elite unit that we are supposed to be.

DEREK LINK: APART FROM AN INCREDIBLE RECORD GOING WAY BACK TO BEST STUDENT AT THE POLICE COLLEGE, GEN LEBEYA IS ALSO AN ACADEMIC WITH FOUR LAW DEGREES. THIS BOOK, UNDERSTANDING ORGANISED CRIME, EMANATED FROM HIS DOCTORATE.

VO: This is sure to serve him well as he tackles the enormous challenge of cleaning up the rot in the Hawks and banishing the damaging legacy of the last permanent Hawks head Berning Ntlemeza, who was dismissed in 2017 after the Pretoria High Court found his appointment was irrational and unlawful.

DEREK LINK: ONE OF THE PERSONAL TRAGEDIES OF THE RASH OF STATE CAPTURE IS HOW DEDICATED OFFICIALS HAVE BEEN REMOVED FROM THEIR POSTS TO ENABLE THE TENTACLES OF CORRUPTION TO EXPAND THEIR GRIP.

BHEKI CELE: Well, things have been said around here to say that there was a lot of political interference with the unit which is unfortunate.

DR JOHAN BURGER: Berning Ntlemeza's at the time when he was Head of the Hawks, one of the first things he did is he replaced almost, I think 8 of the 9 provincial heads of the Hawks.

General Lebeya -- the Hawks' fourth head since its inception in 2009 -- is adamant that under his wing, there'll be no place for political manipulation in the Hawks.

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: Whether they were captured or not, I can't say that one, but I need to assess and determine myself or what have actually happened? What is that which made you to deteriorate from the position that you were at in 2011 to find yourself where you are today?

DEREK: You don't think that politics played a role during the Zuma years?

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: I haven't assessed that one and then I don't want to express my opinion, because my opinion might be wrong. So all what I can say is that the performance is not the same.

VO: General Lebeya is a man who would rather get the job done than point fingers. This may stem from his humble beginnings in rural Limpopo.

BHEKI CELE: He's such a team man, he is a man that has no arrogance, works with everybody and making sure that the work is done.

After he matriculated in 1981, he did a number of odd jobs from being a gardener to a brick-layer in order to survive. But this grandfather of two and husband of 32 years admits it wasn't his childhood dream to become a policeman.

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: I wanted to be a mechanical engineer. But I was not lucky to get accommodated in some of the technical colleges that we had.

VO: After police training, he took the oath in 1984 and began his career as an officer in Hillbrow. In 2014, Lebeya fell foul of then national police commissioner Riah Phiyega. His position as deputy national commissioner in charge of crime intelligence and detective services was made redundant. Instead, Phiyega wanted him to head-up a new research division yet to be formed - but with a demotion in his rank.

DR JOHAN BURGER: I think at the time she knew that he would probably not accept a position where he would be relegated and placed in a position of obscurity almost. And of course he fought this.

After demoting him, Phiyega finally dismissed general Lebeya in 2016. He fought his demotion in rank and dismissal in the Labour Court - and won both cases.
The Labour Court found that Phiyega's actions were "procedurally unfair" and the general was awarded compensation. After he left the police force, he then started to practice as an advocate.

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: it has never been my choice to leave the organisation. I wanted to remain in this organisation.

VO: There are allegations that general Lebeya was sidelined by Phiyega because he was tasked to oversee an investigation into maladministration by the then Crime Intelligence boss, Richard Mdluli in the Crime Intelligence division.

DEREK TO LEBEYA: Allegation of a conspiracy against Richard Mdluli?

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: The Minister at the time established a semi-commission of enquiry and in their finding they have actually said that what we have done in the investigation of those issues that were put before us, is the best that any other officer could have done.

For General Lebeya, that's in the past and he is looking forward -- to how he can restore the Hawks to a unit that yields results.

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: what we are going to be focussing on is crime. And part of the priority crimes that the Hawks is dealing with is serious organised crime, serious corruption and serious commercial crime. So while we deal with the rest of national priority offences, those three that I have mentioned come tops.

MINISTER CELE: The man has arrived. If anybody has lost hope, please bring your hope back now.

END -

PROMO 1: 10"
A new head for the Hawks -- high hopes that General Godfrey Lebeya will turn the tide against crime.

BHEKI CELE/MINISTER OF POLICE: South Africans, have been presented with one of the best sons of South Africa.

PROMO 2: 15"
With a doctorate in law and more than three decades of service in the police, the new head of the HAWKS, General Godfrey Lebeya may be bad news for organised crime.

MINISTER CELE: If anybody has lost hope, please bring your hope back now.

PROMO 3: 15"
DEREK PROMO LINK: The appointment of general Godfrey Lebeya as boss of the Hawks has been widely endorsed, but can he remove all the parasites from the Hawk's nest?

GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: it is a challenge that I'm prepared for.

PROMO 4: 30"
VO: There's a new Hawk soaring high to prey on the country's toughest criminals. His name is Godfrey Lebeya and he is watching closely.

GENERAL LEBEYA: some of the things that I need to be bringing into this job is integrity. I need those who are working with me to understand that corruption is something that can't visit the Hawks.

BHEKI CELE: I believe the Hawks will begin to fly now, the situation now is corrected.

Lebeya, along with Bheki Cele, Gauteng provincial police commissioner Mzwandile Petros, and then Hawks Head Anwa Dramat, were all named by Mdluli in a 2011 letter to Jacob Zuma accusing the officers of colluding to unseat him as head of Crime Intelligence. Mdluli faced fraud and corruption charges related to the abuse of a massive crime intelligence division slush fund for private benefit, including buying luxury cars. Phiyega refused to declassify crucial evidence in the Mdluli matter. The NGO Freedom Under Law said that the failure by Phiyega to declassify the documents had allowed Mdluli to "get away scot-free both at SAPS and in a court of law". Former Gauteng Hawks head Shadrack Sibiya, tasked by Lebeya to investigate the murder of Oupa Ramogibe, who allegedly had an affair with Mdluli's former partner, said the investigation had later cost him his job. Mdluli and his co-accused, former police officer Mthembeni Mthunzi, faced charges of intimidation, kidnapping, assault with the intent to commit grievous bodily harm and defeating the ends of justice. These as well as the other charges relating to the Crime Intelligence slush fund were later withdrawn by acting NPA head Nomgcobo Jiba - who was struck off the advocates roll in 2016. The charges against Mdluli were later reinstated in 2015 following a ruling by the SCA. In 2015, Lebeya was one of five candidates who made it to the initial shortlist of possible new heads of the Hawks. The short-listing panel was chaired by then Police Minister Nathi Nhleko. The desperately under-qualified Berning Ntlemeza, who was not on the shortlist, was catapulted into the job by Nhleko, who then took more than a year to inform Parliament that he had given Ntlemeza the job. Ntlemeza immediately set about eviscerating the directorate of qualified senior staff. He was also responsible for suspending Sibiya in 2015, which was later declared unconstitutional and invalid. Ntlemeza was finally given the boot by former Police Minister Mbalula in 2017, bringing to an end to a shameful and disastrous two years for the DPCI, during which it also hounded then finance Minister Pravin Gordhan on trumped-up charges relating to the SARS "rogue-unit". Now, the rot of corruption is deep and has spread to all levels of society, especially in SOEs like Eskom, Prasa, SARS, to municipalities - all brought to the brink of collapse by corrupt officials and political cronies. Violent crime has spiked, cash-in-transit heists are at a record high. Experts say everyone expect that Lebeya's appointment will bring miracles at a fast speed, but he first needs to sweep clean - look into those appointments that were made due to political influence and set the record straight to be able to build a strong team under him. And then he needs to refocus to rebuild the unit into what it is supposed to do and do well - to investigate priority crime at the highest of levels - no easy task. But he was a deputy commissioner for Crime Intelligence and he was the head of detective services. He knows what it would require. Lt Gen Lebeya, who is highly regarded by his peers, was also one of the candidates to replace Thuli Madonsela as public protector. His appointment as Hawks boss was announced along with a string of other posts, including a permanent head for Crime Intelligence and a permanent National Police Commissioner. Lt Gen Lebeya's appointment follows years of accusations that the elite investigating unit had been politicised. For years organised crime and corruption has been rampant in South Africa and the Hawks, which targets criminal syndicates and other economic crimes, has been accused of been ineffective. Now with a doctorate in law and three decades of service in the police, General Godfrey Lebeya has been appointed to lead this elite crime fighting unit. Can the man who was once in the running for Public Protector, clean up the rot in one of the most important offices in the criminal justice system? Producer: Este de Klerk Presenter: Derek Watts Researcher: Siniketiwe Hlanze Script: PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK PRESENTER: DEREK WATTS EDITOR: ROBIN LEUCI BROADCAST DATE: 17 JUNE 2018 [START WITH SEQUENCE OF VIOLENT CRIMES] South Africans live in fear of the serious violent crimes which continue to threaten society: From armed robberies, murders, car-hijackings, the recent spike in cash-in-transit heists, and the decimation of state-owned enterprises through corrupt officials and state capture [show another short sequence of violent crimes] BHEKI CELE: 2010/2011 people have forgotten about cash-heists, you go and see your stats It was a really rare happening unlike today. when it comes to murders, we are back to 19 000 in the year from 16 000, we are back to daily car-hijacking. Why it has happened, how it has happened, don't ask me, I wasn't there. VO: As part of police minister Bheki Cele's plan to clean up the country's crime fighting units, General Godfrey Lebeya has been appointed as the new head of the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, the Hawks - a man the minister selected to be deputy commissioner in charge of crime intelligence and detective services in 2011 when he was police commissioner. BHEKI CELE: The biggest advantage with him, the man has been almost 32 years on the game, he was once a deputy head, he is not new there, highly decorated when it comes to education, knows the law very well. VO: It's clear that the new Hawks boss has been burning the midnight oil since he took office on the 1st of June. We met this warm and affable career policeman at his office at seven in the evening - the only gap he could find for the interview and the first he's granted to the media since his appointment. [DEREK & LEBEYA MEETING AND SHAKING HANDS] DEREK: General, did you have much sleep over the last two weeks? GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: I must say that I have not. I have been thinking about the task ahead of me, so that kept me awake most of the time. I feel honoured that I've been called again to come and join others who are fighting corruption. BHEKI CELE: He never goes to sleep before he finishes, cleans his desk. He is a man that will never, and whenever when you make the call he will ask is: Do you need me? When you say: Yes! It doesn't matter what time of the day, he will be there. DEREK LINK: WHILE THE APPOINTMENT OF GENERAL LEBEYA HAS BEEN WIDELY ENDORSED AND HIS PEDIGREE IS IMPRESSIVE...THE QUESTION REMAINS...HOW CAN HE GO ABOUT REMOVING THE PARASITES FROM THE HAWKS NEST VO: With refreshing candor, General Lebeya is quick to admit the Hawks he took over is not the elite crime fighting unit it's supposed to be. DEREK: Some say that the country's ability to fight crime has been totally decimated. GENERAL GODFREY LEBEYA: The performance of the Hawks as of now, the latest, is not the same as the performance of the Hawks in 2011. What went wrong? We are seeking answers as of now and I think that when I say I'm doing assessment, I'm also looking at answers and I know that pretty soon, we will to a certain extent know where did we go wrong. DEREK: What are your immediate priorities? GENERAL GODFREY LEBEYA: The immediate priorities are those that is a burning issue to the people of South Africa. I hear and see what the rest of South Africans are seeing. DEREK LINK: WITH THE HAWKS IMPLICATED IN A NUMBER OF SERIOUS CRIMES, ALONG WITH DRAGGING THEIR FEET IN STATE CAPTURE INVESTIGATIONS, THEIR PUBLIC IMAGE IS AT AN ALL TIME LOW AS GENERAL LEBEYA TAKES THE HOT SEAT Dr Johan Burger, senior researcher of the Institute of Security Studies has known general Lebeya for the past 20 years. He says South Africa can be assured that this new Hawks Head will be watching closely and will act decisively against the country's toughest criminals. DR BURGER: The Hawks generally are perceived as inefficient, as corrupt, as also complicit in a number of crimes themselves. Now the new incumbents have to fix the leadership within their various components of the police service and at the same time make them more effective. VO: General Lebeya is determined to restore the image of the Hawks as an elite and successful crime fighting unit. DEREK: what do you feel that you can bring to this job? GENERAL LEBEYA: some of the things that I need to be bringing into this job is integrity. I need those who are working with me to understand that corruption is something that can't visit the Hawks. the community should trust us and that is how we shall obviously be building this elite unit that we are supposed to be. DEREK LINK: APART FROM AN INCREDIBLE RECORD GOING WAY BACK TO BEST STUDENT AT THE POLICE COLLEGE, GEN LEBEYA IS ALSO AN ACADEMIC WITH FOUR LAW DEGREES. THIS BOOK, UNDERSTANDING ORGANISED CRIME, EMANATED FROM HIS DOCTORATE. VO: This is sure to serve him well as he tackles the enormous challenge of cleaning up the rot in the Hawks and banishing the damaging legacy of the last permanent Hawks head Berning Ntlemeza, who was dismissed in 2017 after the Pretoria High Court found his appointment was irrational and unlawful. DEREK LINK: ONE OF THE PERSONAL TRAGEDIES OF THE RASH OF STATE CAPTURE IS HOW DEDICATED OFFICIALS HAVE BEEN REMOVED FROM THEIR POSTS TO ENABLE THE TENTACLES OF CORRUPTION TO EXPAND THEIR GRIP. BHEKI CELE: Well, things have been said around here to say that there was a lot of political interference with the unit which is unfortunate. DR JOHAN BURGER: Berning Ntlemeza's at the time when he was Head of the Hawks, one of the first things he did is he replaced almost, I think 8 of the 9 provincial heads of the Hawks. General Lebeya -- the Hawks' fourth head since its inception in 2009 -- is adamant that under his wing, there'll be no place for political manipulation in the Hawks. GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: Whether they were captured or not, I can't say that one, but I need to assess and determine myself or what have actually happened? What is that which made you to deteriorate from the position that you were at in 2011 to find yourself where you are today? DEREK: You don't think that politics played a role during the Zuma years? GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: I haven't assessed that one and then I don't want to express my opinion, because my opinion might be wrong. So all what I can say is that the performance is not the same. VO: General Lebeya is a man who would rather get the job done than point fingers. This may stem from his humble beginnings in rural Limpopo. BHEKI CELE: He's such a team man, he is a man that has no arrogance, works with everybody and making sure that the work is done. After he matriculated in 1981, he did a number of odd jobs from being a gardener to a brick-layer in order to survive. But this grandfather of two and husband of 32 years admits it wasn't his childhood dream to become a policeman. GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: I wanted to be a mechanical engineer. But I was not lucky to get accommodated in some of the technical colleges that we had. VO: After police training, he took the oath in 1984 and began his career as an officer in Hillbrow. In 2014, Lebeya fell foul of then national police commissioner Riah Phiyega. His position as deputy national commissioner in charge of crime intelligence and detective services was made redundant. Instead, Phiyega wanted him to head-up a new research division yet to be formed - but with a demotion in his rank. DR JOHAN BURGER: I think at the time she knew that he would probably not accept a position where he would be relegated and placed in a position of obscurity almost. And of course he fought this. After demoting him, Phiyega finally dismissed general Lebeya in 2016. He fought his demotion in rank and dismissal in the Labour Court - and won both cases. The Labour Court found that Phiyega's actions were "procedurally unfair" and the general was awarded compensation. After he left the police force, he then started to practice as an advocate. GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: it has never been my choice to leave the organisation. I wanted to remain in this organisation. VO: There are allegations that general Lebeya was sidelined by Phiyega because he was tasked to oversee an investigation into maladministration by the then Crime Intelligence boss, Richard Mdluli in the Crime Intelligence division. DEREK TO LEBEYA: Allegation of a conspiracy against Richard Mdluli? GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: The Minister at the time established a semi-commission of enquiry and in their finding they have actually said that what we have done in the investigation of those issues that were put before us, is the best that any other officer could have done. For General Lebeya, that's in the past and he is looking forward -- to how he can restore the Hawks to a unit that yields results. GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: what we are going to be focussing on is crime. And part of the priority crimes that the Hawks is dealing with is serious organised crime, serious corruption and serious commercial crime. So while we deal with the rest of national priority offences, those three that I have mentioned come tops. MINISTER CELE: The man has arrived. If anybody has lost hope, please bring your hope back now. END - PROMO 1: 10" A new head for the Hawks -- high hopes that General Godfrey Lebeya will turn the tide against crime. BHEKI CELE/MINISTER OF POLICE: South Africans, have been presented with one of the best sons of South Africa. PROMO 2: 15" With a doctorate in law and more than three decades of service in the police, the new head of the HAWKS, General Godfrey Lebeya may be bad news for organised crime. MINISTER CELE: If anybody has lost hope, please bring your hope back now. PROMO 3: 15" DEREK PROMO LINK: The appointment of general Godfrey Lebeya as boss of the Hawks has been widely endorsed, but can he remove all the parasites from the Hawk's nest? GENL GODFREY LEBEYA: it is a challenge that I'm prepared for. PROMO 4: 30" VO: There's a new Hawk soaring high to prey on the country's toughest criminals. His name is Godfrey Lebeya and he is watching closely. GENERAL LEBEYA: some of the things that I need to be bringing into this job is integrity. I need those who are working with me to understand that corruption is something that can't visit the Hawks. BHEKI CELE: I believe the Hawks will begin to fly now, the situation now is corrected.

metadata.Further information: For more than a year the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, better known as the Hawks has been without a permanent head. The unit has been dogged with perception of political interference especially in high-profile appointments for years. The Hawks has had four head since its inception after the Scorpions disbandment in 2009 and adv. Godfrey Lebeya's appointment is regarded as a new dawn within the unit. His appointment comes at a critical time in turning the tide of the endemic corruption of the Zuma years. Lebeya, once sidelined by former SAPS National Commissioner Riah Phiyega, is highly respected. But he will have his work cut out for him rebuilding a directorate that has been put under much suspicion by his predecessor, Berning Ntlemeza. He replaces Lt-Gen Yolisa Matakata, who was appointed acting Hawks head by former police minister Fikile Mbalula in April 2017 after the appointment of Maj-Gen Berning Ntlemeza to the position was ruled to have irregular and unlawful. Matakata had stood in after the controversy around former Hawks head Bernard Ntlemeza. In March 2015, the High Court in Pretoria found that Ntlemeza lied under oath, mislead the court and lacked integrity and honour. The High Court struck his case from the roll, saying his appointment was irrational and unlawful. He was forced to vacate his office after the High Court, in Pretoria, turned down an application by Ntlemeza to turn to the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein in a bid to cling to his position as the head of the Directorate of Priority Crimes Investigation. Following the court ruling, Mbalula called for unity within the police. He said he hoped finality in the Ntlemeza matter brought an end to factionalism within the police. He warned that Ntlemeza is now considered to be on the outside of the organisation and was demanding the officers be professional and reject the idea of being part of what he terms "rogue cabals". Former Minister Mbalula publicly stated he planned to drive out corrupt elements out of the controversial crime intelligence unit. But Ntlemeza's legal woes were far from over. The High Court ruling formed the basis of an application to have his appointment as head of the Hawks set aside on the ground that he was fit to hold the position. Ntlemeza state in a sworn affidavit that former KZN Hawks boss, Johan Booysen was party to the process to appoint his successor and that he was also interviewed as a candidate, but as Booysen pointed out in a supplementary affidavit, this claim was not true. Ntlemeza filed a follow-up statement saying that he had signed an incorrect draft affidavit which included the error, without reading it. Ntlemeza was also accused of attempting to mislead the Supreme Court of Appeal in a statement he made to the SCA to appeal the KwaZulu-Natal High Court's rejection of his appeal in the matter involving Booysen. Ntlemeza made inaccurate comments in an affidavit to the SCA and described the inaccurate comments as a bona fide error. In June 2016, the SCA ruled that Ntlemeza's appointment should be set aside. In his letter to the constitutional court, Ntlemeza said that he was only made aware of the June ruling of the SCA in September. At the time, Booysen said this explanation was incredulous and couldn't be believed, considering that Ntlemeza was a Lieutenant-General who was the head of the Hawks and should know the gravity of deposing to an affidavit. He said for Ntlemeza to claim that he did not read the affidavit made a mockery of the legislation because this would become a convenient excuse for anyone lying under oath in written statements. Further to this, Ntlemeza wrote to the constitutional court for leave to appeal his removal from the Hawks and he also wanted former Police Minister Fikile Mbalula to reinstate him while awaiting the outcome of the Constitutional Court application. In September 2017, Ntlemeza lost his final court bid to overturn his dismissal. The SCA dismissed his application for leave to appeal the decision setting aside his appointment. At the time, the Police Ministiry said Ntlemeza's employment contract was set aside, as if it never existed. Former Police Minister Mbalula said that meant Ntlemeza was considered retired at a lower rank. Praise for Lt Gen Lebeya's appointment streamed in. He comes with an impressive record. Not only has Lt Gen Lebeya been a career policeman for 37 years, he also has four law degrees, was ad advocate with the Johannesburg bar and did his highly-regarded doctorate in organized crime. His thesis flowed to a book about organized crime, on not only academic, but also practical level on how organized crime should be tackled in South Africa. He and another high-ranking officer were caught up in a legal wrangle over the dismissals and they'd won a large settlement after being illegally fired by former top cop Riah Phiyega. But his service was terminated nonetheless. It was because of Mdluli, who was close to Jacob Zuma, that Lebeya was sidelined by Phiyega in 2014 while he oversaw an internal investigation into maladministration in the Crime Intelligence division.
